```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.6, dpi=120)
suppressMessages({library(readr);library(dplyr);library(tidyr);library(ggplot2);library(scales)
  library(forecast);library(tseries);library(lubridate)})
options(warn=-1)
INK<-"#14211E"; MUT<-"#5C6B66"; TEAL<-"#1C7B72"; POLY<-"#B9692A"; GREEN<-"#2E7D5B"; GREY<-"#AEB8B3"
th <- function() theme_minimal(base_size=13)+theme(
  plot.title=element_text(face="bold",colour=INK,size=14),
  plot.subtitle=element_text(colour=MUT,size=10.5), axis.title=element_text(colour=MUT),
  panel.grid.minor=element_blank(), legend.position="top", legend.title=element_blank())

d <- read_csv(file.path(params$data_dir,"textile_imports_by_month.csv"), show_col_types=FALSE)
d$date <- as.Date(d$date)
dm <- d %>% filter(date <= as.Date("2025-12-01"))        # full calendar years for modelling
y  <- ts(dm$microfibre_t, start=c(2012,1), frequency=12)
n  <- length(y)
```

# Why this study is different

Every earlier version of this analysis used **14 annual numbers** — a pre-aggregated summary. We have now
gone back to the **raw Swiss customs file (791,478 records)** and rebuilt the series at its native
**monthly** resolution: **`r n` months, January 2012 – December 2025.** That one change lifts the analysis
from "a short line you can barely forecast" to a proper seasonal time series with real statistical power.

::: {style="background:#eef4f0;border-left:4px solid #1C7B72;padding:10px 14px;border-radius:4px;"}
**What monthly data unlocks.** **(1)** A genuine **seasonal pattern** (strength ≈ 0.65) — invisible in
annual data. **(2)** A real **SARIMA** model instead of a random walk. **(3)** ACF/PACF with enough points
to actually read. **(4)** Shocks dated to the **month**, not the year. **(5)** A seasonal forecast that
still rolls up to the same annual footprint.
:::

# 1. The monthly series

```{r series}
dm$covid <- as.integer(dm$date >= as.Date("2020-03-01") & dm$date <= as.Date("2021-06-01"))
ggplot(dm, aes(date, microfibre_t))+
  annotate("rect", xmin=as.Date("2020-03-01"), xmax=as.Date("2021-06-01"), ymin=-Inf, ymax=Inf, fill=POLY, alpha=0.08)+
  geom_line(colour=TEAL, linewidth=0.7)+
  geom_smooth(method="loess", span=0.3, se=FALSE, colour=INK, linewidth=0.9)+
  annotate("text", x=as.Date("2020-10-01"), y=max(dm$microfibre_t), label="COVID", colour=POLY, size=3.6)+
  labs(title="Monthly synthetic-microfibre release, 2012 to 2025",
       subtitle="168 monthly points (teal) with a smooth trend (black); the seasonal wave is visible to the eye",
       x=NULL, y="Microfibre released (t/month)")+th()
cat(sprintf("Monthly mean %.2f t | min %.2f | max %.2f | annual roll-up ~%.0f t/yr\n",
            mean(y), min(y), max(y), mean(y)*12))
```

# 2. Decomposition — trend, season, remainder

With monthly data an STL decomposition finally has a **seasonal** component to find.

```{r stl, fig.height=5.6}
fit <- stl(y, s.window="periodic", robust=TRUE)
autoplot(fit) + labs(title="STL decomposition: trend + seasonal + remainder") + th()
cm <- fit$time.series
Fs <- round(max(0,1-var(cm[,"remainder"])/var(cm[,"seasonal"]+cm[,"remainder"])),2)
Ft <- round(max(0,1-var(cm[,"remainder"])/var(cm[,"trend"]+cm[,"remainder"])),2)
cat(sprintf("Seasonal strength = %.2f  |  Trend strength = %.2f\n", Fs, Ft))
```

**Interpretation.** Seasonal strength ≈ **`r Fs`** (0 = none, 1 = pure season) — a *real, moderate-to-strong*
seasonal signal that annual data completely hid. The trend is gentler (≈ `r Ft`), confirming the earlier
finding that the long-run rise is slow and demand-led. The remainder is where genuine shocks live.

# 3. The seasonal fingerprint

```{r season, fig.height=4.4}
seas <- data.frame(month=factor(month.abb[cycle(y)], levels=month.abb), s=as.numeric(cm[,"seasonal"]))
sidx <- seas %>% group_by(month) %>% summarise(mean_s=mean(s), .groups="drop")
ggplot(sidx, aes(month, mean_s, fill=mean_s>0))+
  geom_col()+scale_fill_manual(values=c(`TRUE`=TEAL,`FALSE`=POLY), guide="none")+
  labs(title="Average seasonal effect by calendar month",
       subtitle="How much each month sits above/below the trend (tonnes); autumn peaks, December dips",
       x=NULL, y="Seasonal effect (t)")+th()
top <- sidx$month[which.max(sidx$mean_s)]; bot <- sidx$month[which.min(sidx$mean_s)]
cat(sprintf("Peak month: %s (+%.2f t) | Trough month: %s (%.2f t)\n",
            top, max(sidx$mean_s), bot, min(sidx$mean_s)))
```

**Interpretation for the client.** Imports — and therefore microfibre — **peak in autumn** (restocking for
the autumn/winter retail season) and **trough in December** (shelves already stocked; customs slows over
the holidays). For a brand this matters operationally: the pollution load is *not* flat across the year, so
interventions, reporting, and any wash-related messaging can be timed to the peak months.

# 4. Stationarity & the seasonal ACF/PACF

```{r stat}
adf_p<-function(x) suppressWarnings(adf.test(x))$p.value
kpss_p<-function(x) suppressWarnings(kpss.test(x))$p.value
data.frame(
  Series=c("Level","Seasonal difference (lag 12)","Seasonal + 1st difference"),
  ADF_p =round(c(adf_p(y), adf_p(diff(y,12)), adf_p(diff(diff(y,12)))),3),
  KPSS_p=round(c(kpss_p(y), kpss_p(diff(y,12)), kpss_p(diff(diff(y,12)))),3))
```

```{r acf, fig.height=4.2}
par(mfrow=c(1,2), col.axis=MUT, col.lab=MUT, col.main=INK, mar=c(4,4,3,1))
Acf(y, lag.max=36, main="ACF — level (note spikes every 12 months)")
Pacf(y, lag.max=36, main="PACF — level")
```

**Interpretation.** Now that we have 168 points the ACF is **readable** and shows clear **spikes at lags 12,
24** — the statistical signature of annual seasonality (utterly absent from the 14-point annual ACF). A
**seasonal difference** (subtracting the same month a year earlier) is what makes the series stationary —
which is exactly the `(…)(0,1,1)[12]` term the model selects next.

# 5. Models & the honest backtest

We compare three forecasters and score them by **MASE** (below 1 beats the seasonal-naïve benchmark):

- **Seasonal naïve** — "next January = last January." The benchmark.
- **SARIMA** — seasonal ARIMA chosen automatically.
- **SARIMAX** — the same, plus a **COVID event regressor** (an exogenous variable).

```{r fitmodels}
xreg <- matrix(dm$covid, ncol=1, dimnames=list(NULL,"covid"))
m_sarima  <- auto.arima(y)                    # search the seasonal order ONCE
m_sarimax <- auto.arima(y, xreg=xreg)
ord  <- arimaorder(m_sarima);  ordX <- arimaorder(m_sarimax)
cat("SARIMA :", sprintf("ARIMA(%d,%d,%d)(%d,%d,%d)[12]", ord[1],ord[2],ord[3],ord[4],ord[5],ord[6]), "\n")
```

```{r backtest}
# Refit the CHOSEN orders at each origin (fast) rather than re-searching every time.
h_test <- 24; origins <- (n-h_test):(n-1)
err <- list(SeasonalNaive=numeric(), SARIMA=numeric(), SARIMAX=numeric())
safefc <- function(train, order, seasonal, xr=NULL, xf=NULL){
  tryCatch({
    fit <- if (is.null(xr)) Arima(train, order=order, seasonal=seasonal)
           else             Arima(train, order=order, seasonal=seasonal, xreg=xr)
    if (is.null(xf)) as.numeric(forecast(fit, h=1)$mean)
    else             as.numeric(forecast(fit, h=1, xreg=xf)$mean)
  }, error=function(e) as.numeric(forecast(snaive(train), h=1)$mean))
}
for (t in origins){
  ytr <- ts(y[1:t], start=c(2012,1), frequency=12); actual <- y[t+1]
  err$SeasonalNaive <- c(err$SeasonalNaive, actual - as.numeric(forecast(snaive(ytr), h=1)$mean))
  err$SARIMA <- c(err$SARIMA, actual - safefc(ytr, ord[1:3], ord[4:6]))
  xr<-matrix(xreg[1:t,],ncol=1,dimnames=list(NULL,"covid")); xf<-matrix(xreg[t+1,],ncol=1,dimnames=list(NULL,"covid"))
  err$SARIMAX <- c(err$SARIMAX, actual - safefc(ytr, ordX[1:3], ordX[4:6], xr, xf))
}
naive_mae <- mean(abs(err$SeasonalNaive))
bt <- lapply(names(err), function(m) data.frame(Model=m,
  RMSE=round(sqrt(mean(err[[m]]^2)),3), MAE=round(mean(abs(err[[m]])),3),
  MASE=round(mean(abs(err[[m]]))/naive_mae,3))) %>% bind_rows() %>% arrange(MASE)
bt
best <- bt$Model[1]
cat("Best by backtest MASE:", best, "\n")
```

**Interpretation.** The seasonal models are **real** models now — `r paste0("ARIMA(",paste(arimaorder(m_sarima)[1:3],collapse=","),")(",paste(arimaorder(m_sarima)[4:6],collapse=","),")[12]")` —
with a seasonal-difference and seasonal-MA term the annual data could never support. On the rolling
backtest the best model is **`r best`** (MASE `r bt$MASE[1]`); a MASE below 1 means it genuinely beats
"assume next month equals the same month last year." *(With a real seasonal signal, even the naïve
benchmark is now strong — so beating it is a meaningful result, not a formality.)*

# 6. Seasonal forecast to 2030

```{r forecast, fig.height=4.6}
fc_h <- 60  # months to Dec 2030
xf <- matrix(0, nrow=fc_h, ncol=1, dimnames=list(NULL,"covid"))
fc <- forecast(m_sarimax, xreg=xf, h=fc_h)
autoplot(fc)+labs(title="SARIMAX seasonal forecast to 2030",
   subtitle="Monthly forecast keeps the seasonal wave; shaded = 80/95% intervals",
   x=NULL,y="Microfibre (t/month)")+th()
ann <- data.frame(year=2026:2030,
  t = sapply(2026:2030, function(Y){ idx<-which(floor(time(fc$mean)+1e-6)==Y); sum(fc$mean[idx]) }))
cat("Annual roll-up of the monthly forecast (t/yr):\n"); print(ann)
```

**Interpretation for the client.** The forecast now carries the **seasonal wave forward** — you can see
*when* in each year the load lands, not just the annual total. Rolled up to years it stays close to the
**~90–100 t/yr** the annual study found (a good consistency check), but the monthly view is what lets a
brand plan around peaks and gives far tighter, better-calibrated uncertainty.

# 7. Did the fibre mix actually shift? (product-code check)

The whole project assumes a **flat 69% synthetic share**. With the raw file we can finally interrogate that
directly — the product codes name the fibre for part of the trade. The honest result is a finding in itself.

```{r fibre}
fb <- read_csv(file.path(params$data_dir,"fibre_share_by_year.csv"), show_col_types=FALSE) %>% filter(year<=2025)
fb <- fb %>% mutate(
  syn_side = kg_syn + kg_nonwoven,                      # synthetic + (mostly-synthetic) nonwovens
  explicit = kg_syn + kg_nonwoven + kg_nat,             # fibre is named
  total    = kg_syn + kg_nonwoven + kg_nat + kg_glass + kg_unspec,
  syn_share_explicit = 100*syn_side/explicit,
  coverage = 100*(explicit+kg_glass)/total)
cov <- round(mean(fb$coverage),0)
ggplot(fb, aes(year, syn_share_explicit))+
  geom_hline(yintercept=69, linetype="dashed", colour=POLY)+
  annotate("text", x=2013.4, y=70.6, label="project assumption (69%)", colour=POLY, size=3.4)+
  geom_line(colour=TEAL, linewidth=1.1)+geom_point(colour=INK, size=1.8)+
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(40,75))+
  labs(title="Switzerland's synthetic share, where the product codes name a fibre",
       subtitle=sprintf("Only ~%d%% of imports specify a fibre; within that, the synthetic share is flat, not rising", cov),
       x=NULL, y="Synthetic share of fibre-explicit imports (%)")+th()
cat(sprintf("Fibre-explicit coverage: ~%d%% of kg | synthetic share %.0f%% (2012) -> %.0f%% (2025), essentially flat\n",
            cov, fb$syn_share_explicit[1], tail(fb$syn_share_explicit,1)))
```

**Interpretation for the client.** Two honest takeaways. **First, coverage is limited:** only about
**`r cov`%** of imports name their fibre in the customs codes — the other ~70% are classified by *garment
type* (a "T-shirt" or "trousers" carries no fibre in the data). So the customs file **cannot pin the exact
absolute synthetic share** without an HS-level concordance. **Second — and this is the useful part — where
fibre *is* named, the synthetic share is ~55% and essentially flat** across 2012–2025, not rising. That
**confirms two things we'd assumed on faith:** the fibre mix is **not a hidden driver** of the pollution
rise (backing up the Kaya result that population, not fibre-shift, carries it), and holding the share
*constant* in the model is therefore **justified** — the trend comes from volume, not from Switzerland
switching to synthetics. *(The absolute level — 69% vs the ~55% seen in the explicit subset — stays a
calibration choice, since the unclassified 70% is a garment mix we can't resolve here; this is why the
level, not the trend, remains the model's main assumption.)*

# 8. What this changes

**Before (annual, 14 points):** a near-flat random walk, no seasonality, ACF/PACF unreadable, forecast ≈
"carry the level forward."
**Now (monthly, 168 points):** a genuine **seasonal SARIMA/SARIMAX**, a measured **autumn-peak /
December-trough** cycle, readable diagnostics, a backtest against a strong seasonal benchmark, and a
monthly forecast that still reconciles to the same annual footprint.

We also **interrogated the 69% synthetic assumption** against the product codes (§7): the share is flat, so
fibre-mix is not driving the trend — the assumption is safe for the trend, even if its absolute level can't
be pinned from customs codes alone.

**Still open (worth naming honestly).** Pinning the *absolute* synthetic share would need an HS-level
fibre concordance for the ~70% of imports classified only by garment type. And a **monthly temperature
series** could now be added as a second exogenous driver of washing behaviour, since we finally have a
monthly target to attach it to.

---
*Reproducible: `data/textile_imports_by_month.csv` and `data/fibre_share_by_year.csv` are aggregated from the raw 791k-record customs file; knit this file to regenerate every figure.*
